issues.quote: He made his face black. So no one knew him. ... The swineherd took the black off his face. Now he looked like a prince again.
issues.problem: Andersen's disguise is dirt or soot. Here no substance is named, so the text says he coloured his face black to look low-born and removed the black to 'look like a prince again'. A modern reader can easily take this as blackface and as tying dark skin to low status.
issues.fix: "He put dirt on his face and wore old clothes. So no one knew him." ... "The swineherd washed the dirt off his face. Now he looked like a prince again."

issues.quote: "It is only a real rose!" she said. "And it is only a real nightingale. Send it away."
issues.problem: The A1 text never says that the princess wanted a made or toy rose. An A1 reader cannot see why 'real' is a complaint, and this is the point of the whole story.
issues.fix: Add before the quote: "She wanted a toy rose, not a real one."

issues.quote: The Emperor saw the women and went down.
issues.problem: The Emperor's place (the balcony or window) is never given, so 'went down' has no reference point and the scene is unclear.
issues.fix: "The Emperor looked out of his window. He saw the women near the pigs. He went down to them."

issues.quote: "Look after my pigs," said the Emperor.
issues.problem: 'Look after' is a phrasal verb that a beginner may read as 'look behind'.
issues.fix: "You can work with my pigs," said the Emperor.

issues.quote: It could play an old tune.
issues.problem: 'Tune' is not glossed and is outside beginner vocabulary. The next paragraph also needs a clear referent for 'that one'.
issues.fix: "It could play an old song." and later "I know that song!" (instead of "I know that one!")

issues.quote: She stood outside, all on her own.
issues.problem: 'All on her own' is an idiom.

issues.quote: He made his face black. So no one knew him.
issues.problem: 'Knew' in the sense of 'recognised' is easy for an A1 learner to misread as 'no one knew who he was in general'.
issues.fix: "Now no one saw that he was the prince."

notes: "It played every dance in the world" is slightly odd. "It played the music for every dance in the world" is clearer.
Grammar stays within present simple and past simple, and the quiz keys are correct.

issues.quote: He made his face black and put on old clothes. ... He took the black off his face and changed his clothes. Now he was a prince again.
issues.problem: This is the same blackface reading as in A1. The colour is not explained as dirt, and removing it makes him 'a prince again'.
issues.fix: "He put dirt on his face and put on old clothes." ... "He washed the dirt off his face and changed his clothes."

issues.quote: "Then I give him ten," said the Emperor's daughter.
issues.problem: A present simple form used for an offer is not natural English. A reader would stumble on it.
issues.fix: "He can have ten kisses from me," said the Emperor's daughter.

notes: "She wanted a made rose, not a real one" is a little stiff. "She wanted a rose made of silk, not a real one" sounds more natural.
"said the young man's people" would sound better as "said the prince's men".
"He went down" works better if it follows "The Emperor looked out of his window".

issues.quote: He made his face brown and black and pulled his cap down low. ... washed the brown and black from his face
issues.problem: Skin colouring is described with no named substance, so the disguise can read as blackface.
issues.fix: "He rubbed dirt and soot on his face and pulled his cap down low." ... "washed the dirt and soot from his face"

notes: "by the evening he made a pretty little pot" should be "by the evening he had made" or "in the evening he finished".
"or we each keep our own things" would be more natural as "or we each keep what we have".
There are no conditionals or passives. The quiz keys are correct.

issues.quote: He rubbed his face with brown and black ... wiped the brown and black from his face
issues.problem: This is the same problem as in B1. Name the dirt or soot so the disguise cannot be read as darkened skin.
issues.fix: "He rubbed his face with dirt and soot" ... "wiped the dirt and soot from his face"

notes: "just large enough to marry on" is an old translation idiom. It is fine at B2, but some learners may stumble on it.
The wooden shoes are unexplained. A short addition such as "to keep her feet clean in the yard" would help.

issues.quote: He smeared his face with brown and black ... wiped the brown and black from his face
issues.problem: This follows the older translation closely, but out of context it still reads as colouring the skin. The 4+ rating needs the substance named.
issues.fix: "He smeared his face with dirt and soot" ... "wiped the dirt and soot from his face"

notes: "each a little worse than the next" is illogical. Use "each speaking it a little worse than the last".
The C1 text is otherwise literary and faithful, with the musical box, the slippers, the chamberlain and the bolted door all present.

summary: The retelling follows Andersen closely at every level, and all quiz keys are correct. Every level fails 4+ suitability because the disguise is 'making his face black / brown and black', which can read as blackface; naming dirt or soot fixes it. A1 also has unclear logic (why 'real' is bad, and where the Emperor 'went down' from) and a few beginner-blocking words, and A2 has one unnatural line ('Then I give him ten').
